D005-D018_h001.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since the car accident—about two months ago—when I barely survived after a truck ran a red light. Ever since, I keep reliving it. Sometimes, I’m just sitting at home and suddenly I feel the impact all over again—the jolt, the glass shattering. I’ll feel phantom hands grabbing the steering wheel even though I’m alone. It’s like I’m back there. And there are moments I swear I can feel someone pulling me out of the wreckage, but no one’s there.  

It’s not just that. I’ve started feeling like I’m meant for something bigger—like the crash was a sign. I sometimes think I’ve been given a second life for a reason, that I can now sense things others can’t, maybe even protect people from fate. But that doesn’t make sense, does it? I’m a landscape architect—I design parks, not save souls.  

I can’t sleep, I startle at noises, and I avoid driving completely. My husband says I’ve changed. I know these thoughts aren’t normal, but they’re tied to that moment—the crash. It’s like my mind won’t let it go.
D005-D018_h001.options:
A. Bulimia Nervosa
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Schizophrenia

D005-D018_h002.question:
I’ve been seeing things—like shadows of people who aren’t there, sometimes even faces in the cabin during flights. Crew members’ casual jokes feel loaded, like they’re secretly talking about me, sending me signals. I can’t shake the feeling that everything around me means something, that I’m missing a message. 

But it’s been worse since the incident—when our plane had to make an emergency landing after the engine failed mid-flight. I haven’t been the same since. I keep reliving it—the screaming, the oxygen masks dropping, the way the wings trembled. Sometimes I’m back in it completely, like I’m in the cockpit again, heart pounding, feeling the plane drop. These flashbacks come out of nowhere, even when I’m off duty. I wake up drenched in sweat, convinced we’re crashing.

I started avoiding flights at first, but I can't afford to lose my job. Now I’m jumpier, irritable all the time, barely sleeping. My husband says I seem distant. I know the things I see aren’t real, but they feel connected to that flight—the trauma. It’s like my mind won’t let me leave it behind.
D005-D018_h002.options:
A. Bulimia Nervosa
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Schizophrenia

D005-D018_h003.question: I’ve been struggling ever since I lost my job two months ago—well, not just that. It brought back everything from the accident last year, when a colleague died right in front of me at my old warehouse job. I still see it, clear as day—his face, the sound… sometimes I hear him calling my name when no one’s there. Lately, I even hear whispers saying my wife is cheating on me, that she’s been with other men. I know she says it’s not true, but the voices feel so real, and I can’t shake the feeling she’s hiding something. I check her phone, I ask her where she’s been—it’s causing a lot of fights. I used to be steady, supporting my family. Now I jump at noises, I can’t sleep unless I’m exhausted, and when I do, I’m right back at that accident scene. I smell the smoke, hear the sirens—it’s like I’m there. It’s been like this for over a month now. The thoughts about my wife didn’t start until *after* the nightmares and the flashbacks kicked in. It’s like the trauma cracked something open, and now my mind won’t let me trust anything—even her.
D005-D018_h003.options:
A. Bulimia Nervosa
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Schizophrenia

D005-D018_h004.question:
I’ve been having these strange episodes for about two months now. Ever since the accident—when a tree fell and crushed my coworker right next to me—I keep seeing it happen again, like it’s playing in my head. Sometimes I’ll be pruning hedges, and suddenly I’m back there, hearing him scream, feeling the dirt spray on my face. It’s not just memories—it’s like I’m there. And I smell it too… burned rubber and blood, even when there’s nothing around. I know it sounds wild, but I can’t shake the feeling that people are talking about it when they mention accidents or storms—they don’t know me, but I swear they’re hinting at me, like it’s all a secret code.

I’ve been avoiding jobs with big trees. I startle easy now, can’t sleep without nightmares, and I don’t go near the site where it happened. I used to love being outside, but now it feels unsafe. The smells, the flashbacks, the way I interpret every little thing—it’s all tied to that moment. I know the tree didn’t fall on purpose, but my mind keeps looping back, like if I don’t watch for signs, it’ll happen again.
D005-D018_h004.options:
A. Bulimia Nervosa
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Schizophrenia

D005-D018_h005.question:
I’ve been having these awful flashbacks to the night my husband died—over fifty years ago, but it feels like it’s happening all over again. I see his face, hear his voice calling me, and sometimes I swear I feel his hand gripping mine, even though I know he’s gone. It’s like he’s trying to tell me something. Lately, I’ve started believing he’s still trying to reach me from beyond, that he never really left because he loves me too much. I feel his presence in bed at night, like someone’s touching my arm or pulling the blanket, but when I turn, no one’s there. It’s been going on daily for about two months now. 

I haven’t been sleeping. I keep reliving the ambulance, the hospital, the way they covered him with a sheet. I startle at every noise, won’t go out after dark, and I can’t bear to watch anything violent on TV. I used to enjoy the senior group at church, but now I just sit at home, afraid something will trigger another episode. These feelings—of fear, guilt, like I could’ve saved him—are constant. The thoughts about him loving me still, the sensations… they always come right after a flashback. It’s like the past won’t stay past.
D005-D018_h005.options:
A. Bulimia Nervosa
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Schizophrenia

D005-D018_h006.question:
I’ve been off since that accident seven months ago—when the building collapsed during demolition. I was inside, trapped for hours. Since then, I can’t shake the feeling that people are watching me, especially construction crews or even my own partners. I swear they’re wiretapping my phone, maybe working with the city to frame me for something. I’ve stopped going to job sites; I pace oddly when I talk on calls, like I’m reenacting something I can’t remember clearly.

The worst part? I used to love closing deals, driving around the city seeing my projects rise. Now, nothing excites me. My wife says I’ve gone cold. I don’t touch golf anymore, don’t laugh like I used to.

And sometimes—it’s like I’m back there. The dust, the noise, the screams. I see the beams falling, feel the weight—fully real, like it’s happening now. That’s when I lock the doors, convinced crews are coming for me. I know it sounds fractured, but every time I feel this way, it starts with remembering *that moment*. The paranoia, the visions—they always follow the flashback. It’s not random. It’s like the trauma knocks something loose.
D005-D018_h006.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Anorexia Nervosa
    D. Delusional Disorder

D005-D018_h007.question:
I’ve been really off since my car accident seven months ago—when the drunk driver hit us head-on. I was photographing a wedding that night; it was pouring rain. The crash killed the couple in the other car. Since then, I keep *seeing* their faces in the rearview mirror, even when I’m not driving. Sometimes I feel like the camera sees things before they happen—like I’m supposed to capture something tragic, destined or prophetic. My husband says I’ve been rocking back and forth while editing photos, over and over, like I don’t even notice. And I don’t talk much anymore. Words just… don’t feel real.

The worst part is reliving the crash—the smell of wet upholstery, the shattered lens, the silence right after impact. I’ll be at a wedding, smiling for clients, and suddenly I’m back there, hearing screams that aren’t there. I don’t know if I’m having visions or breakdowns, but they always *start* with the memory of that impact. It’s like the trauma pulls the hallucinations from its pockets—same time, every time.
D005-D018_h007.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Anorexia Nervosa
    D. Delusional Disorder

D005-D018_h008.question:
I’ve been a violinist with the symphony for three years, but lately, I can’t even pick up my bow without feeling like something’s tearing through my chest. It started about seven months ago—ever since that night during the concert when the auditorium lights collapsed. I saw a man get crushed right in front of me. Since then, I keep *seeing* it—his face, the sound of the metal cracking, like it’s happening all over again. Sometimes I’ll be tuning my violin and suddenly I’m back there, frozen, sweating.  

I don’t feel like myself. I used to love playing—now I don’t care. Nothing feels good anymore. My hands... they just keep moving on their own, tapping, twisting, like they’re stuck in loop. I can’t stop them. I’ve told myself I’m meant to do something huge—like I can *channel* the trauma into some masterpiece no one’s ever heard. But I know that’s not real.  

The worst part? These visions—they come right after a flashback. Like the trauma brings the voices, the ideas, the movements. It’s not random. It’s always tied to that moment. I don’t think I’m broken in the way they’re suggesting. I think I’m stuck in it.
D005-D018_h008.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Anorexia Nervosa
    D. Delusional Disorder

D005-D018_h009.question:
I’ve been a plumber for twelve years—wrench in hand, under sinks, in tight crawl spaces. Ever since that gas line explosion seven months ago, though, I can’t seem to get my head right. I was right there when it blew—I saw one of my crew get thrown across the basement. I keep reliving it. Outta nowhere, I’ll smell burning again or see flashes like it’s happening all over. Sometimes I freeze up completely, just sitting on the side of the road in the truck, unable to move. My wife says I stop talking for hours, just stare at the wall like I’m not even home.  

There are moments—rare, but strong—where I feel like I survived for a reason. Like I’m meant for something bigger. I can’t explain it, but I feel chosen, like I’ve got some kind of power after making it through. But then the horror comes back: nightmares, jumping at sounds, avoiding job sites with gas lines. That explosion changed me. These blank spells, the silence, the visions—they only started after that day. They’re tied to it. I don’t think I’m crazy—but I keep re-living the worst moment of my life.
D005-D018_h009.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Anorexia Nervosa
    D. Delusional Disorder

D005-D018_h010.question: I’ve been struggling since my husband passed in that terrible car accident seven months ago. I was in the car too—I still see it: the headlights coming at us, the sound… sometimes it feels like it’s happening all over again, right here. I get flashes so vivid I swear I can smell the smoke. It’s like I’m back there. Since then, I’ve felt… disconnected. Like the world isn’t real, or worse—sometimes I think everything is going to just vanish, that life has no point, that we’re all headed for ruin. I’ll catch myself giggling at nothing, like a little girl, when I’m talking to clients—it just slips out, and they get uncomfortable. I feel it too—I’ve become quieter, don’t know what to say anymore. Words feel heavy. I used to love showing homes, talking to people, but now I barely speak during listings. I keep thinking the accident was my fault, that the world’s punishing me. But those visions, the laughing, the silence—they all started *after* the crash. It’s like my mind hasn’t left that road.

    D. Delusional Disorder

D005-D018_h011.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since that warehouse collapse last year—we pulled three victims out, one was just a kid. Since then, I keep seeing things… like the smell of smoke suddenly fills the room, or I hear screams when no one else does. My wife says I’ll just freeze, sometimes raise my arms like I’m shielding myself from falling debris—don’t even realize I’m doing it. I know it sounds crazy, but I swear people on the news are sending me coded messages about the incident, like the anchor’s glancing at the camera just for me. It’s not that I think I’m someone special—it’s like the world is replaying that moment, trying to make me remember. 

I wake up drenched, heart pounding, like I’m back in the smoke. I avoid crowds, won’t even watch TV scenes with fires. My wife says I’ve changed—distant, jumpy. These episodes, the postures, the thoughts—they’ve been happening most days for about four months now. But it all ties back to that call, that fire. It’s not random. It’s like my mind won’t let me leave it behind.

A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D005-D018_h012.question: I’ve been having these intense flashbacks—like I’m right back in that car crash, hearing the metal crunch, feeling it all over again. I jump at noises—dropped weights, loud music—anything sudden. I’ve been avoiding anything that reminds me of that day, but it’s hard because my mind keeps replaying it. The thoughts about my girlfriend… I know they might not make sense, but they feel tied to everything that happened—like somehow, the crash made me lose control of everything, and now I’m losing her too. D005-D018_h013.question:
I’ve been struggling for about four months now, ever since I found my ex-husband’s things at my workshop—clothes, tools, notes to someone else. I know he’s seeing someone, maybe even living with her, but every time I try to talk to him, he lies. That’s not even the worst part. I keep reliving that night last winter when he shoved me against the workbench during one of our fights—the smell of sawdust, the drill spinning on the floor, his voice yelling… I see it so clearly sometimes, even when I’m awake, like it’s happening again. I’ve started sleeping in the back room of my shop because the noise outside reminds me of that moment.

I catch myself giggling at odd times—during silence, or even at funerals—like I’m twelve again and don’t have to make sense. My hands shake, and I’ve locked the shop door at night, convinced he’s out there, watching. I know it sounds strange, but the jealousy—I just *know* he’s betraying me—feels tied to that moment he put his hands on me. It’s like every suspicious thought, every silly outburst, drags me back to that cold garage, afraid and small.
D005-D018_h013.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D005-D018_h014.question:
I’ve been a documentary director for over twenty years—used to thrive on high-pressure shoots in conflict zones. But since that ambush in Syria four months ago, everything’s changed. I saw my cameraman die right next to me. I keep reliving it—sudden, vivid flashbacks where I feel the heat of the explosion again, hear the gunfire like it’s happening now. Sometimes they come with hallucinations—I’ve *seen* his blood on my hands when they’re clean. 

After that, something shifted inside. I started believing I was meant to survive for a reason—that I’m some kind of prophetic witness, chosen to expose hidden global truths no one else can see. I’ve struck these rigid, almost theatrical poses during interviews, holding them for minutes, like I’m channeling something beyond me. My ex-wife says I look like I’m performing.  

I can’t sleep without nightmares, I’m jumpy all the time, and crowds make me panic. But the grand ideas, the posturing—it all started right after the attack. It’s like my mind is trapped between what happened and what I now believe I have to do because of it.
D005-D018_h014.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D005-D018_h015.question:
I’ve been struggling a lot lately—ever since my ex-husband died in that car crash four months ago. I was the first responder on the scene… I recognized his face, but part of me still thinks he’s alive, hiding somewhere, cheating on me with one of his old coworkers. I know it doesn’t make sense—medically, I *know* he’s gone—but I keep seeing her, this woman, in the hospital halls, like she’s watching me. I’ll hear her name muttered… sometimes I repeat things the patients say without realizing, like my mouth moves on its own.

The nightmares are constant—reliving the crash, the smell of gasoline, his voice calling my name. I startle at sirens now. I avoid driving past the intersection. I haven’t slept through the night since it happened. I feel on edge every shift, hyperaware, like danger’s waiting. Some days I feel numb, like I’m floating above the ward, watching myself work. 

The delusions… they always tie back to him, to the crash, to the betrayal I can’t prove. It’s not just random—it’s like my mind keeps returning to that moment, rehashing it, punishing me. Whatever’s happening, it started *after* I pulled him from the wreckage. That’s when the world changed.
D005-D018_h015.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Major Depressive Disorder

D005-D018_h016.question:

The doctors say my heart’s failing, that I’m rotting inside—no matter how many tests they run, I know they’re right. 

I wake up sweating, my skin crawling like bugs are under it. I don’t talk much anymore—what’s the point? Words just twist in my head, coming out jumbled, like “sparks in the dark” or “clocks talk fast”—don’t even make sense when I hear 'em myself. 

It’s been like this off and on for three months solid. The nightmares come back, sudden and sharp, like I’m living that moment again. I jump at shadows and avoid the east tunnel where it happened. D005-D018_h017.question: I’ve been struggling since the lab accident last year—my colleague died, and I still see it. The paranoia, the tastes, the way I speak—it’s all tied to that. I’m not losing touch with reality; I’m trapped inside one part of it.

D005-D018_h018.question:
I’ve been having these awful flashbacks—like I’m back *there*, in that alley after the attack last year. Sometimes I feel hands grabbing my arms, even when I’m alone in my studio. I know it’s not real, but the fear is. I flinch, I scream… my assistants think I’m losing it.

D005-D018_h019.question:

D005-D018_h020.question:

D005-D018_h020.options:

D005-D018_h021.question:

D005-D018_h022.question:

D005-D018_h022.options:

    C. Schizophrenia
    D. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D005-D018_h023.question:

D005-D018_h023.options:

D005-D018_h024.question:
